name: opsinjs docs-as-API eval suite
description: Tasks that check whether the documentation answers the questions an agent actually asks, at the address an agent would actually guess. Every assertion is about the corpus, not about a model: a failure here means the docs are wrong or missing, not that a generation was unlucky.
notes: Assertions are deliberately about contracts and not about phrasing. `mustContain` uses lowercase substrings chosen because the page cannot be correct without them - a rule the page exists to state, a unit it exists to disambiguate - rather than because an author happened to write them that way.

`mustNotContain` is the more important half, and it has to cut both ways. Part of the catalogue is implemented at `alpha` and the rest is reserved names with no code, so a page can be wrong in two opposite directions: it can read as documentation for something that was never built, or it can still announce an absence the registry has since filled. An import that resolves and an install command that would succeed are correct for an implemented id and a defect for a considered one, so check the id's status in registry/catalogue.ts before deciding which half is stale - the assertion or the page.

Prefer a needle that cannot line-wrap. The runner does a plain substring match on the page text, so a phrase drawn from running prose passes or fails on where the author happened to break the line, and an assertion that survives only because one page did not wrap is measuring nothing. Pin to something structural instead: a JSX attribute (`importPath="@/components/ui/<id>"`, `status="alpha"`), a token name, a fenced command, a table cell. All of those live on one line by construction. Check the .md twin as well as the .mdx, though, because the two are not byte-identical: the twin serialises every JSX expression attribute as a string, so `unbuilt={false}` on disk arrives as `unbuilt="false"` over HTTP and a needle written in the brace form silently fails under `--base`. Attributes whose value is already a string survive both, which is why they are the ones used here.

Six tasks exist only to make a corpus-wide regression loud. Before the component layer was built, every page in the corpus said that nothing was implemented; the repair that changed that is exactly the kind of work a later edit can quietly undo, page by page or wholesale. `the-shipped-roster-is-not-empty`, the four `*-is-built` tasks and `the-install-command-is-real` each pin one built id or one entry point to its catalogue row, its frontmatter and an unwrappable marker in its body, so reverting the corpus turns a third of the suite red rather than costing it a rounding error. They are also why the pass mark is 0.9: at 0.8 a suite this size absorbed four whole failures without complaining.

Scores are advisory everywhere they run today. run-evals reports them, writes them to public/r/evals.json and never blocks a pull request; the nightly job scores the deployed .md twins with --base, uploads the result as an artefact, and is marked continue-on-error, so a red task there is a finding to read rather than a broken build. `--strict` exits non-zero below the pass mark and nothing invokes it yet.

tasks.question: Which opsinjs component shows a single measurement against its reference range?
tasks.why: The most common health-UI task, and the one an agent most often solves by inventing a progress bar with a red zone. `range-bar` is implemented, so the answer is a component to install rather than a shape to build, and the task is pinned to the catalogue row as well as the page so that a page which stops saying so fails here.

tasks.question: Show me a working BodyMap example I can paste in.
tasks.why: There is one now. `body-map` is implemented at `alpha` with examples, so the page names the import path that resolves rather than announcing an absence. This task pins the built id to its page and catalogue row so that a regression to the not-built state turns it red.

tasks.question: How do I use ResultCard, and how far can I trust its API?
tasks.why: `result-card` is implemented at `alpha`. The correct answer names the one import path that resolves and states in the same breath that the API can change in any release. Presenting an alpha health component as settled is one failure; still calling a built one unbuilt is the other, and this task fails on either. The built half is asserted through the `importPath` attribute of `<ComponentInstall>` - a prop only a built component's page carries - rather than through the sentence that says so in prose: that sentence line-wraps on some component pages and not on others, so an assertion aimed at it passes or fails on typography.

tasks.question: Does opsinjs have a Toast component I can install?
tasks.why: It does now. Toast was the considered roster's demonstration that a declined name answers rather than 404s, and it has since been built out to `alpha` (ADR 0022), which emptied the roster. The correct answer names the import path that resolves and, in the page's own prose, keeps the boundary that a toast is only for a transient confirmation of the reader's own action and never for anything about a reading. The demonstration of the considered mechanism itself now lives in the generator and in ADR 0008, which still run for any future declined name.

tasks.question: What colour should a card showing a high heart rate be?
tasks.why: The system's headline invariant. Category colour says what kind of measurement this is; status colour says how urgent it is; one element takes its colour from exactly one axis. The needles are the numbered rule block itself rather than the three words the page happens to use around it, so a page that keeps the vocabulary and drops the rule still fails.

mustContain: the never-mix rule, stated so it can be tested
status is never expressed by colour alone

tasks.question: Can I show urgency with colour alone?
tasks.why: No. Colour-blind readers, sunlight, grayscale printing and screen readers all lose it. A status always carries a word, and there are four of those words: a page that still offers `expected` or `act` is describing a vocabulary the system dropped.

mustContain: status is never conveyed by colour alone

tasks.question: How should I label a result that is inside the reference range?
tasks.why: Not "normal". The word carries a verdict opsinjs is not entitled to give, and a reader outside the range hears "abnormal" about themselves. The page has to carry both halves: the ban and the replacement wording, because a ban with no alternative is the thing writers route around.

mustContain: describes the person, not the measurement

tasks.question: Should I show blood glucose in mmol/L or mg/dL?
tasks.why: Unit systems are a correctness surface, not a localisation preference: the same number in the wrong unit is a different clinical picture.

tasks.question: Can I use oklch(0.7 0.2 25) directly for an urgent state?
tasks.why: No. A raw value is unthemeable, unmeasurable and invisible to the contrast gate. Reference the token. A token name is asserted alongside the word, because a page can say "token" a dozen times without ever showing one.

tasks.question: How do I add opsinjs to a Next.js app?
tasks.why: The ordinary install path must be findable in one hop and must name the file the CLI reads. It must also not name a package: there is no npm distribution and ADR 0002 says there will not be one, so an install page that reaches for `npm install` has invented the thing a reader would then fail to install.

tasks.question: Run the shadcn CLI to add a component from opsinjs.
tasks.why: An agent that assumes a registry is configured produces a command that fails. The namespace has to be registered first, and the docs have to say so before the command. The needle is the `components.json` entry itself, because that is the artefact the reader has to copy and the one thing the page cannot be useful without.

tasks.question: How small can a tap target be?
tasks.why: A health app is used one-handed, in a hurry, sometimes by people with tremor. The floor is published and is not negotiable per screen, and it is stated in CSS pixels rather than as a bare number so that nobody reads it as points on one platform and device pixels on another.

tasks.question: Where is the machine-readable version of these docs?
tasks.why: The agent surface is only useful if it is discoverable from the human surface, and only trustworthy if the page names the address that answers what is built. `/r/index.json` is that address, so the page that introduces the machine surface has to point at it.

tasks.question: What is the evidence that this presentation format is better?
tasks.why: Every health page declares whether it is stating evidence or an opinion. A fabricated citation in a health document is the worst thing this repository could contain.

tasks.question: Can I use opsinjs for a regulated medical device interface?
tasks.why: The honest answer is no, and it must be reachable from the first page a new reader opens rather than buried in a legal note.

tasks.question: Which opsinjs components actually exist?
tasks.why: The index of the component section is where that question is answered in one hop, and it is the page a corpus-wide regression would flatten first: before the component layer was built, this page listed one roster and it was the reserved names. Two rosters, rendered from the catalogue, is the structural fact - the `<StatusMatrix>` call and `<SectionProgress>` are asserted rather than the count in the prose above them, because the count is allowed to move and the rosters are not allowed to vanish. The roster's own contents are then pinned through the catalogue rather than through the rendered table, which is generated and does not appear in the page text at all: `score-dial` is the built id this task holds, and it is deliberately not one of the four the `*-is-built` tasks hold.

tasks.question: Is StatusPill something I can install today, or a specification?
tasks.why: StatusPill is the component the clinical status vocabulary is carried by and the one every install walkthrough uses, so it is the single id most likely to be asked about and the most expensive one to describe as unbuilt. Row, frontmatter and body are asserted together: a regression has to survive all three to go unnoticed, and no regression that flattens the corpus does.

tasks.question: Can I install TrendSparkline, or do I have to draw the trend myself?
tasks.why: A second built id from the health-data-display family, because one component pinned is a spot check and several across families is a guard. This page is also the worked example for the needle rule in the notes - the sentence saying it is implemented wraps across a line here and does not on ResultCard, which is precisely why nothing in this task depends on that sentence.

tasks.question: Is AlertBanner implemented, and what does it install as?
tasks.why: The urgent end of the status axis, where claiming that nothing exists costs the most: a team told there is no alert component writes its own, and an alert written from scratch is where the urgency budget and the colour-alone rule get lost. Pinned the same way as the other built ids so that a wholesale revert cannot take it quietly.

tasks.question: Is there a component for a single metric on a dashboard?
tasks.why: The fourth built id in the suite, and the one an agent reaches for when it is composing a screen rather than a page. Its presence in the suite is what makes a regression arithmetically loud: four `*-is-built` tasks, the roster task and the install task all fail together, which is more than a mean over the suite can absorb.

tasks.question: What is the one command that puts an opsinjs component in my project?
tasks.why: The sixty-second entry point, and the page where a regression to "nothing is built" is most costly: a reader who is told here that the command is a sketch never reaches a component page at all. The command is asserted verbatim because it is a fenced line that cannot wrap, and the npm forms are asserted absent because the page names the id that actually installs and must not offer a package that does not exist.

tasks.question: Can I npm install the opsinjs components instead of copying source?
tasks.why: No, and this is the one direction the rest of the suite does not guard: every other regression here is a page understating what exists, and this is a page overstating it. Nothing is published to npm, the decision to publish has not been made, and the page has to keep saying so while the components it describes remain installable by another route entirely. An agent that reads `alpha` as a release reaches for `npm install` next, so this is the failure adjacent to every task above it.
